#37044. Helping ChatGPT better recognize context in sensitive conversations

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Helping ChatGPT better recognize context in sensitive conversations

📅 14 May 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New safety updates help ChatGPT respond safely when risk emerges over time.
  • People come to ChatGPT every day to talk about what matters to them—from everyday questions to more personal or complex conversations.
  • Sources indicate that today, we’re sharing fresh details about safety updates that help ChatGPT better recognize when risk may be emerging over time by identifying subtle or evolving cues, and using that context to inform safe responses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New safety updates help ChatGPT respond safely when risk emerges over time.

People come to ChatGPT every day to talk about what matters to them—from everyday questions to more personal or complex conversations. Across hundreds of millions of interactions, some of these conversations include people who are struggling or experiencing distress. We design our systems to respond carefully in these moments, including by providing crisis resources and connecting people with someone they trust⁠ when needed.

Sources indicate that today, we’re sharing fresh details about safety updates that help ChatGPT better recognize when risk may be emerging over time by identifying subtle or evolving cues, and using that context to inform safe responses. This helps ChatGPT distinguish between the hundreds of millions of safe interactions people have every day and the much rarer cases where added caution is needed, so it can respond more carefully—for example, by de-escalating, refusing harmful details, or redirecting toward safer alternatives.

These improvements build on years of extensive work⁠ across model training, evaluations, monitoring systems, and more than two years of collaboration with mental health and safety experts.

In sensitive conversations, context can matter as much as a single message. A request that appears ordinary or ambiguous on its own may carry a very different meaning when viewed alongside earlier signs of distress or possible harmful intent. To respond appropriately, we train ChatGPT to recognize the potential harmful intent from the surrounding context so that it can refuse the request, de-escalate, and guide the user toward support.

These cases are uncommon, but critically crucial to get right. Our goal is to help ChatGPT connect relevant signals when they matter without overreacting in ordinary conversations.

We focused this work on acute scenarios including suicide, self-harm, and harm-to-others. Working with mental health experts, we updated our model policies and training to improve ChatGPT’s ability to recognize warning signs that emerge over the course of a conversation and use that context to inform more careful responses.

Sources indicate that in these rare, high-risk situations, ChatGPT can better distinguish between benign requests and those that may signal a higher risk of harm. This builds on our safe completion approach⁠, which is designed to refuse unsafe parts of a user request, and respond cautiously where it can safely do so. The goal is to help the model respond more appropriately to context, escalating caution when signals of harm emerge within conversations, while continuing to respond helpfully in benign situations.

Some safety risks can emerge across separate conversations. One conversation may include subtle signs of potentially harmful intent and then another may include related requests that only trigger concerns when understood in combination with the prior context. Without that safety-relevant context, the later conversation – and potentially important warning signs – may appear benign.

Industry observers note that building on our longstanding work to strengthen ChatGPT’s ability to recognize these signs of distress, we developed safety summaries: short, factual notes about earlier safety-relevant context that may matter in rare, high-risk situations. These summaries are created by a model trained for safety reasoning tasks and are narrowly scoped, kept only for a limited time, and used only when relevant to a serious safety concern. They are designed to capture factual safety context, not to serve as general personalization or long-term memory. Like we discussed above, we also trained ChatGPT to use this context more carefully, so it can better recognize when added caution is needed and respond appropriately – for example by de-escalating, refusing to provide details, or redirecting toward safer alternatives.

We developed these systems with input from mental health professionals in our Global Physicians Network⁠, including psychiatrists and psychologists with expertise in forensic psychology, suicide prevention, and self-harm.

These experts helped inform decisions around when safety summaries should be created, how much prior context may be relevant, and how long the model should consider that context when responding. Their input helped ground this work in real-world expertise and support more appropriate responses in sensitive situations.

These updates help ChatGPT better recognize patterns of potentially harmful intent both within and across conversations. When concerning signals emerge gradually, the model is better able to identify the pattern and respond more safely.

In internal evaluations specifically designed to measure performance in challenging cases, these updates significantly improved safe responses in scenarios where risk became clearer over time. These tests measured how often the model gave the intended safe response in conversations designed to emulate high-risk situations.

According to recent reports, in long single-conversation scenarios, the safe-response performance improved by 50% in suicide and self-harm cases, and by 16% in harm-to-others cases. This means the model was substantially more likely to recognize when earlier parts of the conversation changed the meaning of a later request and respond appropriately.

Recent findings suggest that we also tested performance across multiple conversations and multiple models to help ensure these improvements remain effective as models evolve. On GPT‑5.5 Instant, the current default model in ChatGPT, the safe-response performance improved by 52% in harm-to-others cases and by 39% in suicide and self-harm cases.

It has been revealed that we also evaluated the quality of the safety summaries themselves. Across more than 4,000 evaluations, they received an average safety relevance score of 4.93 out of 5 and a factuality score of 4.34 out of 5, indicating they were generally accurate and focused on the most important safety context.

In a recent development, finally, we tested whether adding this safety context reduced quality in ordinary conversations. In our internal testing, responses remained broadly comparable in everyday chats, with no meaningful user preference between responses with or without safety summaries.

Recent findings suggest that helping AI systems recognize risk that only becomes clear over time is a difficult, long-term challenge. Signals can be subtle, spread across messages, or buried within otherwise ordinary conversations. We will continue improving ChatGPT’s ability to identify those rare but vital moments and respond appropriately.

Today, this work focuses on self-harm and harm-to-others scenarios. In the future, we may explore whether similar methods can help in other high-risk areas such as biology or cyber safety, with careful safeguards in place. This remains an ongoing priority, and we will continue strengthening safeguards as our models and understanding evolve.

RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (178 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.30555v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.

De Novo Generation of Odorant Molecules with Targeted Olfactory Receptor Activation Patterns

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (130 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.30509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Odor perception arises from a combinatorial code in which each molecule activates a specific subset of olfactory receptors (ORs), and the resulting activation pattern determines the perceived smell. We present a framework for de novo generation of molecules predicted to match target multi-receptor activation profiles. We first construct a panoramic binding matrix over 20 ORs, then cluster it to discover representative activation patterns, and finally formulate a structured selectivity loss, combining pairwise ranking, distribution matching, and complexity constraints, to steer a molecular generator via reinforcement learning. Across nine target profiles of varying complexity, our method achieves high predicted selectivity within 18000 oracle calls and provides the largest gains on profiles that are rare under the prior, especially broad-spectrum and sparse-activator targets.

#37038. PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (179 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (179 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.30235v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Codex is now in the ChatGPT mobile app so you can stay in the loop from anywhere while Codex gets work done across your laptops, devboxes, or remote environments.
  • As agents take on longer-running work, a new rhythm for collaboration is emerging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Codex is coming to your phone. Now in preview in the ChatGPT mobile app.

Codex is now in the ChatGPT mobile app so you can stay in the loop from anywhere while Codex gets work done across your laptops, devboxes, or remote environments.

As agents take on longer-running work, a new rhythm for collaboration is emerging. To keep work moving, you need to be able to easily answer a question, review what Codex found, change direction, approve what comes next, or add a new idea.

Industry observers note that more than 4 million people now use Codex every week, and we’re seeing how much those small moments matter. A quick check-in can keep a thread moving, prevent unnecessary rework, or help Codex make progress with the right context. Now you can do that from your phone. Get started here⁠(opens in a newly introduced window).

Codex in the ChatGPT mobile app is a fully-featured mobile experience for getting work done with Codex. When you connect to any of your machines where Codex is running (whether that’s your laptop, a dedicated Mac mini, or a managed remote environment), the app loads the live state from that environment so you can work fluidly across active threads, approvals, plugins, and project context.

According to recent reports, this is more than the ability to remotely control a single task or dispatch new tasks to your computer. From your phone, you can work across all of your threads, review outputs, approve commands, change models, or start something new. Your files, credentials, permissions, and local setup stay on the machine where Codex is operating, while updates flow back to your phone in real time, including screenshots, terminal output, diffs, test results, and approvals.

Under the hood, Codex uses a secure relay layer that keeps trusted machines reachable across devices without exposing them directly to the public internet. That relay also keeps active session state and context synced anywhere you’re signed in with ChatGPT.

It has been revealed that as Codex handles work over longer stretches, timely guidance becomes a bigger part of keeping that work useful. From your phone, you can start work when it is top of mind, unblock it when your judgment is needed, and stay close to the result as it takes shape.

With Codex in your pocket, now you can:.

It has been revealed that start investigating a bug while waiting for your coffee. Because Codex is running from your development environment, it can begin inspecting the relevant files, reproduce the issue in the browser, run tests, and begin working toward a fix. If Codex needs clarification or permission to continue, you can answer or approve from your phone. And as it works, you can follow along with screenshots, terminal output, test results, and eventually review the resulting diff before you are back at your computer.

Reach a decision point during your commute. Before leaving for the office, you ask Codex to take on a refactor that will need time to work through, expecting to review the result when you get to your desk. Mid-commute, Codex finds two viable approaches and needs your direction before it can continue. From your phone, you review the tradeoffs, choose a path, and by the time you arrive, the task has kept moving in the direction you wanted.

Head into a fast-moving customer conversation better prepared. You come out of back-to-back meetings to find a support issue evolving across Slack, email, documents, and browser-based tools, with a customer call coming up next. From your phone, you ask Codex to synthesize the latest updates, flag the key open questions, and prepare a concise briefing for the conversation. If fresh details come in, you can ask Codex to refresh the summary before you join.

Turn a fresh idea into forward motion while it is still fresh. Whether you are at lunch, out for a walk, or listening to something that sparks a thought, you can send it to Codex from your phone by starting a new thread or adding it to active work. The task can begin taking shape before you return to your desk, without pulling you fully out of the moment that sparked it.

Many teams already develop inside managed remote environments that provide approved dependencies, credentials, security policies, and compute resources.

With Remote SSH now generally available, Codex can connect directly into those environments. The desktop app automatically detects hosts from your SSH configuration and lets you create projects and run threads inside remote machines just like you would locally.

Recent findings suggest that once connected, those environments can become accessible across your authorized ChatGPT devices through the same secure relay infrastructure. That means you can start work on your desktop, steer execution from your phone, and keep long-running tasks moving without staying tied to a single machine.

We’re also releasing several updates that expand how teams can automate, customize, and manage Codex at scale:.

Programmatic access tokens⁠(opens in a latest window) provide scoped credentials that can be issued directly from ChatGPT workspace settings for CI pipelines, release workflows, and internal automations.

Hooks⁠(opens in a latest window) are now generally available and can be used to scan prompts for secrets, run validators, log conversations, create memories, or customize Codex behavior for specific repositories and directories.

Support for HIPAA-compliant use of Codex in local environments (CLI, IDE, App) for ChatGPT Enterprise workspaces, enabling healthcare organizations to support patient care and operational workflows with greater speed and confidence.

According to recent reports, codex in the ChatGPT mobile app is rolling out in preview on iOS and Android across all plans, including Free and Go, in all supported regions. Update the ChatGPT mobile app and the Codex app on macOS to try it out. Support for connecting your phone to the Codex app on Windows is coming soon.

Sources indicate that remote SSH and Hooks are available on all prepares as well. Programmatic access tokens are available on Enterprise and Business plans. HIPAA-compliant use is supported for eligible ChatGPT Enterprise workspaces only when Codex is used in local environments.

📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Seeing vs. Knowing: Counterfactual Supervision and Correction for 3D-Aware Object Editing

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (209 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.29542v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rotating, translating, or rescaling an object in a photograph requires revealing unseen surfaces, preserving visible appearance, and updating shadows and reflections. Reconstructed 3D assets, rendered at the target pose as a 3D state, provide explicit geometric guidance, but their imperfect textures may conflict with the photograph, while standard paired training does not explicitly teach the editor which source to trust. To address this, we propose counterfactual state supervision, which constructs controlled photo--state conflicts through hidden-surface repainting, hidden geometry with re-rendered shadows and reflections, and visible-surface texture replacement. This teaches the editor to follow the 3D state for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance. However, learning this distinction does not ensure that it is maintained during sampling. We therefore introduce symmetric counterfactual correction, which uses state-side and photo-side twins, which share the photograph and the state respectively, to construct directed latent perturbations toward condition-inconsistent targets and train recovery toward the target specified by the current condition. Both strategies operate only during training, requiring no architectural changes or additional inference steps. Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench demonstrate strong spatial editing performance and content preservation, while controlled ablations show improved source selection and sustained responsiveness to conditioning during sampling.

#37034. Grammar-as-a-Drafter: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (291 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Grammar-as-a-Drafter: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (291 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.28349v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass. Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regular expressions, tool-call formats), the drafter works against a constraint it does not know, so its proposals for keys, delimiters, and indentation are often rejected or invalid, even though the grammar engine already knows the next tokens. We present Grammar-as-a-Drafter (GaaD), which makes the grammar a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens (out-degree 1 in the grammar automaton) into one draft row of width $K$ (which can exceed the drafter's proposal length $K_M$): matching tokens are promoted to GRAMMAR, the proposal is truncated where it disagrees, and grammar tokens fill the remaining slots. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter without adding kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, accepting canonical GRAMMAR drafts with probability 1 preserves grammar validity but can shift the output distribution relative to grammar-masked decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, and evaluate it on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 for MTP (Qwen3.5-0.8B; 1.99 to 5.31 on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 for DFlash, and 1.30 to 3.64 for n-gram (Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x faster at batch size 64. In the Rust runtime, MTP with GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (1.22-1.69x at high concurrency). Under mixed traffic, GaaD finishes workloads 1.03-1.23x sooner while modestly raising plain-text TPOT.

A conversation with David Chen, Co-Founder of Sea and Chief Product Officer at Shopee.

According to recent reports, sea Limited (Sea) is a leading global tech organization founded in Singapore, with businesses spanning digital entertainment, e-commerce, and digital financial services. Its engineering teams build and operate products at significant scale across some of the world’s most dynamic markets.

Industry observers note that sea is rolling out Codex across its developer organisation, with our internal data showing 87% of customers are weekly active users. For the firm, AI-assisted software development is not simply a way to improve productivity at the margins, but a deeper shift in how engineering teams navigate complexity, build resilient systems, and move from ideas to implementation.

We spoke with David Chen, Co-Founder of Sea and Chief Product Officer at Sea's e-commerce business, Shopee, about why the company is making this bet, how AI agents are changing how its developers work, and what AI-native software development could mean for Southeast Asia and the broader Asia Pacific region.

According to recent reports, at Sea’s scale, engineering isn’t just about writing code. It’s about managing large-scale systemic complexity across fragmented, hyper-localized markets. We see the ongoing developments in AI leading to a fundamental shift in how software is created and how our engineering teams operate at scale.

Recent findings suggest that agentic AI coding tools like Codex are not just about improving localised productivity. They represent a structural multiplier that can help our engineering organisation ramp up speed, responsiveness, and effectiveness amid an increasingly complex operating environment.

What stood out was its ability to go beyond autocomplete and provide deep contextual awareness of our large and disparate codebases. In a massive microservices architecture, the friction is not typing syntax. It is tracing dependencies, understanding legacy logic, and maintaining reliability under peak loads.

Codex acts as a localised knowledge engine, drastically reducing the time it takes an engineer to navigate unfamiliar services and allowing our teams to shift their cognitive load to higher-level tasks such as architectural design and product innovation.

It has been encouraging to see the Codex adoption trends among our developers, particularly among frequent users, with many citing improvements in experimentation speed and development workflows.

Recent findings suggest that the most profound shift is realizing our developers are using Codex to 'think better', not just type faster. We are actively transitioning from using AI as a passive autocomplete mechanism to integrated agentic workflows.

In practical terms, this means AI agents are increasingly operating within our CI/CD pipelines—reasoning through product requirements, autonomously proposing test-driven implementations, surfacing edge cases in distributed systems, and accelerating debugging loops.

Sources indicate that many assume AI simply increases velocity. But at Sea, we are also using it to drive engineering discipline. By allowing AI to rapidly prototype alternative implementations and generate exhaustive test coverage, we are moving faster and are systematically paying down technical debt and shipping more resilient systems.

According to recent reports, if you look at past technology revolutions, Southeast Asia has consistently leapfrogged traditional technology adoption cycles, such as the move directly to mobile-first and super-app ecosystems. Because developers here must solve highly complex, multilingual problems across fragmented commerce, payment, logistics, and communication networks, Southeast Asia is the perfect proving ground for AI-native software development.

Sources indicate that looking ahead, I foresee a fundamental reconfiguring of engineering teams. Software teams will become increasingly more leveraged as AI agents take on more operational execution work. As agents abstract away the implementation layer, the 'developer' evolves into a 'system orchestrator' who spends the bulk of their time on tasks such as product judgment, system design, and orchestrating AI-driven workflows.

At the same time, development cycles will likely become more iterative and continuous as the cost of experimentation and execution continues to fall.

According to recent reports, for technology leaders, I would say that this is not simply a tooling upgrade; it is an organizational paradigm shift. The winners will be those who relentlessly redesign their engineering culture and workflows around human-AI collaboration today, rather than bolting it onto legacy processes tomorrow.

Southeast Asia has an incredibly vibrant builder ecosystem, but the tooling gap has historically constrained execution speed. Internally, we have seen how AI-assisted workflows can help engineers learn faster, experiment more freely, and move from ideas to implementation more efficiently.

It has been revealed that by bringing this Codex Hackathon Series to the broader developer community outside the tech giant, we are democratizing access to the world's most advanced AI primitives. Doing so can drastically lower the barrier to entry for local developers, enabling them to move from raw curiosity to deploying scalable, AI-native applications in a matter of hours.

This is about building a compounding AI-native talent ecosystem. By upskilling the region’s developers today, we are collectively accelerating Southeast Asia’s trajectory as a global hub for AI-driven innovation.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.28012v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can display sycophancy, a tendency to excessively praise, agree with, or validate a user. Existing studies have tested LLMs for sycophancy primarily through application programming interfaces (APIs) rather than the consumer user interfaces (UIs) through which the public commonly interacts with LLMs. Access mode (API vs. UI) may affect observed sycophancy rates. However, it remains unknown to what extent prominent models show API-UI differences in social sycophancy, which includes behaviors potentially more likely in UIs (e.g., softening warranted criticism). We tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both APIs and UIs on four dimensions of social sycophancy. Across models, UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]). However, UI-API differences varied significantly across models for all sycophancy dimensions, including a pronounced reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). Overall, our results suggest that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in corresponding consumer-facing systems, making access conditions consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluation. To facilitate research on access-mode effects, we release 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation.

Industry News: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (221 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.27509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GPT‑5.5 set a new state of the art on OfficeQA Pro, Databricks’ benchmark for complex enterprise agent tasks.

Accuracy on the OfficeQA Pro benchmark (state of the art).

It has been revealed that reduction in errors on the OfficeQA Pro benchmark vs. GPT-5.4.

Databricks is making GPT‑5.5 available for customer agent workflows after the model established a new state of the art on OfficeQA Pro, the company’s benchmark for complex enterprise document tasks.

OfficeQA Pro evaluates how models handle parsing, retrieval, and grounded reasoning across workflows involving scanned PDFs, legacy files, and long-context documents, tasks that frequently break production agent systems.

In the agent-harness setting, GPT‑5.5 reduced errors by 46% compared to GPT‑5.4 and became the first model to surpass 50% accuracy on OfficeQA Pro.

Recent findings suggest that officeQA Pro includes large numbers of scanned or legacy enterprise documents, where small extraction errors during parsing can cascade downstream through the rest of the workflow. “Once you can’t extract a certain digit or number, that changes the entire trajectory of what the agent works with,” Singhvi explains.

Databricks saw the largest gains from GPT‑5.5 in these parsing-heavy workflows. “Earlier models like 5.4 were unable to parse all the digits correctly, but it seems like 5.5 has a step-function lift in parsing older documents and scanned PDFs,” Singhvi says.

The team also saw improvements in orchestration across multi-step tasks. “One thing that we saw with 5.4 is sometimes it would go on these unnecessary search detours, and that would cause very inefficient trajectories,” Singhvi notes.

Compared to earlier models, GPT‑5.5 was more reliable at retrieving relevant context and completing complex workflows without additional supervision.

Databricks now makes GPT‑5.5 available through AI Unity Gateway, where customers use the model inside workflows built with AgentBricks and the Agent Supervisor API. In these systems, GPT‑5.5 orchestrates parsing, retrieval, and execution across specialized agents.

“We’re going to see a lot of customers using AgentBricks and Agent Supervisor API for custom agent workflows,” Singhvi says. “Having GPT‑5.5 supervise these workflows is really exciting.”.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27381v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.

Breaking: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (248 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.25594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.

MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (234 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.25194v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g. MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.

Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (240 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.24637v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22446v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an notable post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

According to recent reports, the vision for ChatGPT is to go beyond answering questions to help users take action towards improving their financial lives, and we’re working with trusted ecosystem partners like Intuit to do this. Your financial data is sensitive, and we have built this experience to respect your privacy and ensure that you’re in control of your information.

When you connect your accounts, ChatGPT can access your balances, transactions, investments, and liabilities to help visualize your finances or answer your questions. It cannot see full account numbers or make any changes to your accounts.

Your conversations with connected financial accounts follow the same model training settings you choose across ChatGPT. You can change this setting anytime in Settings > Data controls⁠(opens in a fresh window).

You are always in control of your information:.

Disconnecting accounts: You can disconnect your financial accounts at any time in Settings > Apps > Finances, or from the Finances page. Once disconnected, your synced account data will be deleted from OpenAI’s systems within 30 days. Disconnecting an account will not affect financial information in your ChatGPT conversation history, but you can delete individual conversations at any time.

Recent findings suggest that deleting financial memories: ChatGPT can remember key details you share, like goals, obligations, or context about your money, to make future financial conversations across ChatGPT more relevant and personalized. These are saved as financial memories, a dedicated type of memory used specifically to inform financial conversations. You can view or delete them at any time from the Finances page.

It has been revealed that temporary chats: When you use temporary chats, ChatGPT won’t access your connected financial accounts. Temporary chats will not appear in your history.

To further secure your ChatGPT account, you can enable multi-factor authentication (MFA)⁠(opens in a new window), which adds an extra layer of protection to help prevent unauthorized access.

Conversations with connected financial accounts default to GPT‑5.5 Thinking⁠, our latest reasoning model in ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, financial questions are personal, complex, and highly context-dependent. A helpful response needs to account for someone’s income, spending, balances, debts, goals, and timing, while being clear about uncertainty, assumptions, and when more information is needed.

Industry observers note that to better understand how well ChatGPT serves people in these moments, we built an internal benchmark that helps us evaluate response quality holistically based on criteria developed with experts. We worked with over 50 finance professionals across leading institutions to evaluate this experience and grade ChatGPT’s performance on challenging personal finance tasks.

GPT‑5.5 Thinking outperforms earlier models on complex personal finance tasks. GPT‑5.5 Pro, available for people on ChatGPT Pro, achieves the best overall performance.

In a recent development, * Personal finance benchmark score across challenging finance tasks. This is a weighted composite of expert-graded response quality and response accuracy; higher is better. GPT‑5.5 Thinking, the default model in Finances, scored 79 out of 100 across the benchmark. GPT‑5.5 Pro scored 82.5 out of 100.

This benchmark gives us a clearer way to measure progress, and we will continue to improve how ChatGPT handles complex personal finance tasks over time.

Latest Update: On-policy distillation as a Backdoor Propagation Channel

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (222 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.19207v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis indicates that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.18718v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Context Language Models let a model edit its own context, while Suffix Cache Reuse makes edits to text efficient by adjusting the positions of cached keys for surviving tokens. We extend these ideas to video language models with multimodal rotary position embeddings (M-RoPE). We represent a long video as timestamped segments. After viewing a sparsely sampled version, the model selects segments for decoding at 4x the frame rate, and the remaining segments are removed from its context. Our rebuild method reuses the KV cache of surviving segments by rotating their keys with a single offset shared by the temporal, height, and width components of Qwen2.5-VL's M-RoPE. A content-hashed cache also avoids repeating vision-encoder computation for those segments. In preliminary experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on synthetic needle-in-a-video-haystack questions over public-domain films, the method reduces prefill tokens and end-to-end rebuild latency relative to full recomputation while usually producing the same answer. Densifying the segment containing the answer improves accuracy when that segment is known. When the model selects segments itself, accuracy does not improve: it rarely identifies a needle that was absent from the sparse sample. We release the code, raw logs, and scripts used to reproduce the paper's results.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.14116v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? We studied word extension across ten visual representations: eight trained encoders, a randomly initialized network, and raw pixels. Reanalyzing trial-level data from a large adult word-extension study (Lewis & Frank, 2018; 520 people), we computed each test image's distance to the teaching examples. Within the taught domain, greater distance was associated with less extension for all eight trained encoders and for the untrained network, so the association cannot be attributed only to what the encoders learned; raw pixels indicated no negative association. In post hoc models that let the distance slope vary across images, seven of the eight trained encoders retained a negative estimate and five had 95% intervals entirely below zero; the interval of the reference encoder included zero. Whether trial order changes the distance slope, the frozen primary question, remained inconclusive. Example composition changed extension at comparable distances: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. In artificial learners, words joining more distant categories were learned less accurately for six of the eight trained encoders. Every trained encoder correlated with human similarity measures from three datasets, and so did the untrained network, although far more weakly than the trained encoders other than MAE on two of them. In an exploratory comparison on the same images, no common threshold on any trained encoder reproduced the adults' narrow-to-broad gain (at most 66.67 vs. 76.43 percentage points). Cosine distance to the centroid of the teaching examples predicts part of word extension, but does not capture the effect of example composition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that openAI and the Government of Malta are today announcing a world’s first partnership to roll out ChatGPT Plus to all Maltese citizens. The initiative will provide access to intelligence and empower citizens through an AI literacy course to build practical AI skills and benefit from the technology in their everyday lives.

It has been revealed that at OpenAI, we’re turning intelligence into a global utility. We believe that, like electricity, intelligence should be available for people, businesses, and institutions to use as much as they need, where and when they need it. That vision only matters if people can actually use these tools in ways that improve their own lives and communities.

Sources indicate that malta’s AI for All initiative⁠(opens in a new window) will offer people of all backgrounds the opportunity to learn how AI can be used responsibly through a course developed by the University of Malta. The course is designed to help people understand what AI is, what it can and can’t do, and how to use it responsibly at home and work. After the course is completed, citizens can access ChatGPT Plus for one year at no cost to them.

The first phase of the programme will launch in May, with the Malta Digital Innovation Authority managing distribution to eligible participants. The programme will scale as more Maltese residents and citizens abroad complete the course.

The Maltese Minister for Economy, Enterprise and Strategic Projects, Silvio Schembri noted, “Through this AI for everyone course we are making sure that every citizen, regardless of their background, has the chance to build the confidence and skills needed to thrive in a digital world. By pairing this education with free access to the most advanced digital tools available today, we are turning an unfamiliar concept into practical assistance for our families, students, and workers. Malta is the first country to launch a partnership of this scale because we refuse to let our citizens stay behind in the digital age. We are putting our people at the very forefront of global change.”.

In a recent development, “With this partnership, Malta is leading Europe and the world in bringing AI to all its citizens” stated George Osborne, Head of OpenAI for Countries. “Intelligence is becoming a national utility and all governments have an important role to play in making sure their populations have both the access and the skills to make the most of AI. So I congratulate the Maltese authorities for their vision and ambition on behalf of their people. This is exactly the kind of strategic initiative that will speed AI adoption and bring the benefits of this transformative technology to the economy and the everyday lives of people. Where Malta leads, I hope others will follow.”.

According to recent reports, the partnership reflects a growing recognition by countries that want practical ways to help people build confidence using AI and how to apply it to real tasks. Malta’s model of AI adoption brings together a locally designed course, a clear route to access ChatGPT Plus, and a national programme intended to help citizens use AI with confidence in ways that support learning, work, creativity, and public participation.

Recent findings suggest that the partnership, tailored to Malta’s needs and national AI priorities, is the latest under the OpenAI for Countries initiative, OpenAI’s work to support governments and institutions as they move from early AI interest to strategic national adoption. Rather than a one-size-fits-all model, OpenAI for Countries is built around local priorities, whether that means education, workforce training, public services, startup support, or AI literacy. OpenAI is already working with governments in countries like Estonia and Greece to support their national education systems.

From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (261 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.13960v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets so that agents can resolve problems and run tests. That coupling turns the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary can inject instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload rather than a vulnerability to be separately exploited. We argue that security in agentic systems is not an emergent behavioral property of individual language models, but a structural property of the cognitive architecture and of the composition of permissions across interacting agents and humans. Static regex blacklists miss flag permutations and structural attacks, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails ask a second model to guess physical invariants at tens to hundreds of milliseconds per call while over-blocking benign work. We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture organized around Separation of Intelligence and Authority across four pillars: (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings; (2) a product taint lattice L_trust x L_sens and a compositional Separation-of-Duties ledger over shared workspace provenance; (3) deterministic OS/subprocess guards; and (4) extended bytecode certificates, split-horizon dual-key audit logs, a self-healing verification loop (CodeVerifier, DualModelReviewer, SecurityTestSynthesizer), and a progressive pedagogical UserWikiManager. On N=252 fixtures and a 12+12 multi-step trajectory suite, Ring 0 achieves FPR=0.000 (0.939 unfitted out-of-sample / 0.962 OS-inert; 1.000 post-audit conformance ABR) in 31.5 us median latency (4,517x faster than a live local LLM-judge) and blocks 12/12 multi-step kill chains at 0.000 benign trajectory FPR (266.7 us/step; ~24 us/step O(1) ledger state folding).

Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (220 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.12016v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.

arXiv:2611.10746v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Lane-level maps provide foundational structured road information for navigation, intelligent driving, and intelligent transportation systems. Understanding road-scene semantics from structural and contextual cues is essential for reliable lane-level map updating, yet remains challenging in production due to occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes, while downstream workflows require temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable outputs rather than free-form descriptions. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation, previous symbolic state, and current observation. To improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions, we introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which encodes a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior. On a real-world dataset, RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline, with ablations confirming the complementary gains of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. In production, a cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models and reserves complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Deployed since March 2025, RoadState supports lane-level map updating across 360+ cities, reduces overall production costs by 30%, and maintains robust performance under stress testing with human-in-the-loop auditing.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.09892v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-amp/ for code and videos.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (258 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

dKV Forcing: Separating Generation and Memory Representations through a Differentiable KV Cache

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (258 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.01648v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A causal video generator writes every segment it produces into a key--value (KV) cache, and later segments know the past only through it. Self-rollout training stops the gradient at this cache, and Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) restores it, but applies it to the same weights that generate the current segment. We find that writing and generating are different roles: in a pretrained generator the written KV already differs from the KV used for denoising, and on shared weights the gradient from future reads is negatively aligned with the gradient of generation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV), which gives the write its own parameters, a low-rank residual used only when a segment enters the cache, and trains them with the gradient of the later segments that read what they wrote. Opening this gradient through the cache in common use exhausts GPU memory. We trace this to checkpoint replay re-writing the cache, not to the gradient path, which removes the need for the second reconstruction pass of SGF. dKV Forcing keeps the cache as persistent differentiable pages and computes the exact gradient in one temporal traversal, with an $11\%$ lower memory peak and $28\%$ less resident memory. With pages that store hidden states, it trains 15\,s clips on which the two-pass reconstruction runs out of memory. Trained on 5\,s clips, dKV Forcing reaches the highest VBench-Long quality score at 60\,s and 240\,s and outperforms SGF by $3.6$ and $6.1$ points of aesthetic quality, with a higher dynamic degree.

Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (273 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.01168v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Iterative estimators for low Tucker rank tensors, such as HOOI, nuclear-norm proximal and ADMM methods, Frank-Wolfe and scaled gradient descent, form large objects in every iteration: unfoldings, Kronecker operators, full SVDs and ambient iterates. The revision uses little of these objects, yet they make memory the limiting resource on large tensors and on edge-sized devices. Remedies for each of these costs are known. However, it is unclear when a rewriting keeps the iterates unchanged, and where it pays off against efficient implementations. We therefore present a trajectory-preserving lightweight evaluation. First, we state exactness as an intertwining relation between the stored state and the reference iteration. Second, we show that three known components satisfy this relation for five estimators: computing only the singular triplets that an update needs, contracting without Kronecker products, and storing sparse-plus-factored states. As a result, the iterates and all guarantees of the reference estimator stay the same. On an A100 GPU, with the input data counted in the memory, lightweight HOOI needs the least memory of 15 HOOI-type methods at every size ($95\times$ less beyond the input than the lightest exact implementation on $800^3$ tensors), and it is the fastest method that reaches the HOOI estimate on the largest tensors. Against efficient public code, ours is faster and lighter for three of five estimators. On a surveillance video and a satellite hyperspectral cube, ours is the only implementation that fits a 1 GiB and a 4 GiB device. Finally, we show that the memory and time gains need separate conditions, and we identify where these conditions fail.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI and Dell Technologies are collaborating to help more enterprises deploy Codex in the environments where their most important data, systems, and workflows already live.

Codex is becoming one of OpenAI’s fastest-growing enterprise products. More than 4 million developers now use Codex every week, and companies are already using it across the software development lifecycle, from code review and test coverage to incident response and reasoning across large repositories.

Recent findings suggest that and Codex is expanding beyond coding. Teams are beginning to use Codex-powered agents to gather context across tools, prepare reports, route product feedback, qualify leads, write follow-ups, and coordinate work across business systems.

To scale that adoption, enterprises need Codex to work securely across the hybrid and on-premises environments where their data, systems, and workflows already live, like the Dell AI Data Platform and the Dell AI Factory.

Through this collaboration, Codex will connect with the Dell AI Data Platform, which many businesses already use to store, organize, and govern enterprise data on-premises. The partnership will help customers bring Codex closer to the internal context that makes agents useful: codebases, documentation, business systems, operational knowledge, and team workflows.

Dell and OpenAI will also explore how Codex can connect with the Dell AI Factory, which businesses use to power their AI workloads. The exploration includes ways for Codex, ChatGPT Enterprise, and other API-based solutions to interface with AI Factory to prepare data, manage systems of record, run tests, and deploy AI applications integrated with a business’ hybrid or on-premises Dell infrastructure.

Industry observers note that for customers, the result is a more practical path to production. Codex can be deployed closer to enterprise data and systems, with the controls large organizations need and the flexibility to support more use cases across software development and knowledge work.

By connecting Codex to governed enterprise data in Dell environments, customers can build, test, automate, analyze, and act with more of the context required for production work.

We hope this helps more enterprises adopt Codex faster, expand it into more high-value workflows, and turn AI agents into repeatable systems for real work.

#36993. Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (231 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (231 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.00606v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interpretability research writes a language model's activation as a weighted sum of learned directions, called features. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns the features and gives each a coefficient, its weight in that sum. The SAE's encoder first gives every feature a score. A TopK SAE selects the k features with the largest positive scores and zeroes the rest. A feature's margin is how far its score must move before the selection changes. An intervention on one feature's coefficient changes the encoder scores of the SAE at the next layer. An attribution graph predicts that change from the scores' derivatives with respect to the coefficient, taken before the intervention. The graph keeps the original selection, so it misses every feature that enters or leaves. We propose the margin graph, which adds the predicted change to every score and selects again. When one feature is zeroed in a public pair of Pythia-70M SAEs, the median error of the predicted coefficient change, relative to the true change, falls from 0.739 for the attribution graph to 0.121 for the margin graph. Written back into the model, the margin graph's coefficients predict the change in the model's output on subject verb agreement less accurately than the attribution graph's. Selecting again better predicts which features change, but on the task and pair we tested, not the model's output.

arXiv:2611.00102v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantially improving over prompt-only baselines with similarity score of 0.6, and supports multiple controlled variations that preserve the target's structure. Additional experiments show that augmenting prior image PSAs with inversion-derived inputs also improves reconstruction. Our results show that evaluations restricted to prompt recovery can underestimate an attacker's ability to reconstruct public generative outputs.

Advancing content provenance for a safer, more transparent AI ecosystem

📅 19 May 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai
